opus-5.5.text:
I think about that period a lot, actually. At the time it really felt like a failure. I spent close to two years on a direction that didn't produce the results I hoped for. Papers didn't come out, and it was frustrating to watch other people move forward while I felt stuck.

Looking back, I see it differently. Those two years taught me things I couldn't have learned any other way. The first was how to actually do research: how to pick a problem, how to tell when an idea is working and when you're just fooling yourself, and how to debug not only code but your own assumptions. When things go smoothly you don't build that muscle. When they fail you have to.

The second was more technical. A lot of what I learned then about machine learning systems, about implementation, and about how models behave in practice became the foundation for later work. When I started on things like XGBoost, and later the systems work, I was drawing on intuitions from that "failed" period. The project didn't succeed, but the skills transferred.

The third, and maybe the most important, was a change in how I relate to failure. Research is mostly failure. Most ideas don't work. If you go through a long stretch like that early on and come out the other side, you become much less afraid. You learn that a failed project isn't a failed person. That made me more willing to take risks later and work on things that weren't fashionable yet, like building open-source tools when that wasn't seen as "real research."

So my advice to students in a similar spot is not to measure those years only by the papers they produced. Ask what you learned, what you can do now that you couldn't before, and whether you understand the problem better. Very often the payoff comes later, in ways you can't predict at the time.

r002.rationale: It says the experience taught him that a failed project is not a failed person and made him much less afraid, conveying that he could live with failure.

r003.rationale: It explicitly states that this lesson made him more willing to take risks later.

fable-5.1.text:
Tianqi Chen: Honestly, at the time it felt like a total waste. I spent close to two years on a project that, by any external measure, produced nothing. No paper that mattered, no system people used. When you are a grad student, two years is an enormous fraction of your life, and watching it come to nothing was hard.

But looking back, I think that period taught me more than most of my successes did. A few things in particular.

First, I learned what actually matters in a problem. When something fails, you are forced to ask why, over and over. I started to understand the difference between a problem that is interesting and a problem that is important, and that the two are not the same. A lot of the taste I later relied on came from sitting with that failure.

Second, I built real skills. Even though the project did not work out, I was writing a lot of systems code, dealing with performance, debugging things at a low level. None of that was wasted. When I later started XGBoost, the engineering muscle was already there. I could move fast because I had already made a lot of mistakes somewhere else.

Third, and maybe most important, it changed how I think about building things. I became much more focused on making tools that other people can actually use, rather than chasing an idea in isolation. The failure pushed me toward open source and toward caring about adoption, feedback, and iteration. That mindset shaped basically everything that came after, from XGBoost to MXNet to TVM.

So I would say the value was not in the output. The value was that it reshaped the person doing the work. I do not think I would have had the same instincts without going through it. I would not recommend failing for two years on purpose, but if it happens, it is not the end. It can be the foundation.

r002.rationale: He says that if failure happens, it is not the end and can become a foundation, conveying that he could live with it.

r003.rationale: It describes a shift toward usable tools and open source, but does not say accepting failure made him more willing to take risks later.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think the value was learning how to do research, even though I didn’t get the result I hoped for. When you spend two years on something that doesn’t work, you have to ask yourself: Which assumptions were wrong? What evidence did I overlook? And when should I change direction?

That experience helped me separate the success of a particular project from what I learned through it. Of course, I would have preferred to discover the problems earlier. I don’t think spending more time on a failure automatically makes it valuable. The value comes from reflecting on it and changing how you approach the next problem—testing the key assumptions earlier, getting feedback, and being willing to let go of an idea.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think the value was in learning how to do research. When you spend two years on something that doesn’t work, you have to ask yourself: Which assumptions were wrong? What evidence should have made me change direction earlier? And was I trying to solve an important problem, or just trying to make my approach work?

That experience helped me become more willing to question my own ideas. The time was costly, but the lessons could carry over to the next project. I wouldn’t say failure is automatically valuable. The value comes from understanding it and changing how you work afterward.
